CoRe-GNN: Multilevel Message passing
on Coarsened graphs

Antonin Joly Affiliation: CNRS, IRISA, Rennes, FRANCE Email: antonin.joly@irisa.fr    Nicolas Keriven Affiliation: CNRS, IRISA, Rennes, FRANCE Email: nicolas.keriven@cnrs.fr    Aline Roumy Affiliation: INRIA, Rennes, FRANCE Email: aline.roumy@inria.fr
Abstract

Training Graph Neural Networks on large graphs is challenged by the memory cost of storing all node representations across layers. We show that several existing scalable approaches can be written as structured modifications of the GNN propagation matrix, providing a unified perspective that exposes their respective limitations. In particular, graph coarsening replaces it by a low-rank approximation that enables spectral guarantees but assigns uniform representations to clustered nodes, while Cluster-GCN restricts the propagation matrix to intra-cluster connections that allow efficient batching but sever long-range information. These are complementary failures of the same decomposition of the graph into groups of nodes. To obtain the best of both worlds, we propose CoRe-GNN, which performs both propagations in parallel at each layer: a coarsened inter-cluster term capturing long-range structure, and a local intra-cluster term preserving per-node discriminability. We prove that CoRe-GNN inherits analogous approximation guarantees to those of graph coarsening, and introduce a natural cluster-based batching scheme that scales to graphs with millions of nodes. On node classification benchmarks spanning homophilic, heterophilic, large-scale, and long-range graphs, CoRe-GNN outperforms both graph coarsening and Cluster-GCN baselines. Notably, CoRe-GNN reaches competitive accuracy on long-range tasks, while remaining memory-efficient through batching.

1 Introduction

Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) [30, 20, 2] have established themselves as the dominant paradigm for learning on graph-structured data. GNNs are deep architectures on graphs that rely on the Message-Passing paradigm [12]: at each layer, the representation Hi(l)∈ℝdlH^{(l)}_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{l}} of each node 1≤i≤N1\leq i\leq N, is updated by aggregating and transforming the representations of its neighbors at the previous layer {Hj(l−1)}j∈𝒩⁡(i)\{H^{(l-1)}_{j}\}_{j\in\mathcal{N}(i)}, where 𝒩⁡(i)\mathcal{N}(i) is the neighborhood of ii. In most examples, this aggregation can be represented as a multiplication of the node representation matrix H(l−1)∈ℝN×dl−1H^{(l-1)}\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times d_{l-1}} by a propagation matrix S∈ℝN×N{S}\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times N} related to the graph structure, followed by a learnable linear transformation. This aggregation can be expressed compactly as: starting from initial node features H(0)∈ℝN×d0H^{(0)}\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times d_{0}}, a GNN with KK layers computes

H(l)=σ(SH(l−1)θ(l)),l=1,…,K,H^{(l)}=\sigma\left({S}H^{(l-1)}\theta^{(l)}\right),\qquad l=1,\ldots,K, (1)

where σ\sigma is a pointwise activation function and θ(l)∈ℝdl−1×dl\theta^{(l)}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{l-1}\times d_{l}} are learned parameters. Classical choices include S=D−1​AS=D^{-1}A (mean aggregation) or the normalized adjacency S=(D+I)−1/2(A+I)(D+I)−1/2S=(D+I)^{-1/2}(A+I)(D+I)^{-1/2}, which corresponds to the classical GCNconv layer [20]. Note that we do not include skip connections here for later ease of exposition. For the rest of the paper, unless otherwise precised, we set S=(D+I)−1/2(A+I)(D+I)−1/2S=(D+I)^{-1/2}(A+I)(D+I)^{-1/2} as in [20].

Training a GNN (1) on a graph of NN nodes requires storing the intermediate representation of each of the KK layers, a memory cost that grows linearly with the number of nodes NN, saturating standard GPU memory for large-scale graphs [14, 13]. This memory bottleneck affects not only training but also inference of the network on such graphs. Unlike in most machine learning settings, naive node batching does not decompose the computation in (1): the representation Hi(l)H^{(l)}_{i} of node ii at layer ll depends on the features of its entire ll-hop neighborhood. For graphs with low average path length, this neighborhood grows rapidly with depth. As emphasized by [36], in OGBN-products [14] the 4-hop neighborhood of one node is in average ≈0.6​M\approx 0.6M nodes (25%25\% of the full graph), leading to memory issues on GPU. This scalability bottleneck has motivated two main families of approaches: sampling-based methods, which truncate the ll-hop neighborhood to a fixed budget per layer, and compressed-graph methods, which train the GNN on a structurally reduced version of the original graph. In this paper we focus on the latter.

Compressed-graph methods and their limitations.

Compressed-graph methods trains the GNN on a structurally reduced version of the original graph. Among them, graph coarsening [25, 22, 19, 7, 5, 17, 16] maps the original nodes to so-called supernodes, forming a smaller graph that retains some properties of the original graph. While, all these methods train the GNN on the coarsened graph, they may differ in how they perform inference at test time. Some [22, 19, 5, 7] apply the learned weights directly to the original graph at inference time. However: a) they generally lack guarantees that these weights transfer well to the original structure, and b) some graphs might even be too large for inference. Other works [17, 16] evaluate entirely within the coarsened space, ensuring consistency between training and inference, and this is the method that we adopt here. However, a fundamental limitation of this approach is that all nodes mapped to the same supernode share the same prediction, which might be limiting especially in heterophilic situations.

In parallel, sparsification approaches restrict S{S} to a sparser version computed once as preprocessing. Cluster-GCN [4] takes the converse approach to graph coarsening: rather than collapsing nodes across clusters, it restricts the GNN to intra-cluster connections only, replacing S{S} by a block-diagonal restriction. In addition to saving (some) memory, the main advantage of this approach is to easily allow for batching during training, which is normally known to be rather problematic for GNNs: kk-hop subgraphs are required around each batched nodes, which can easily be the entire graph. By forming disconnected subgraphs that can be independently loaded, Cluster-GCN solves this problem. However, the main limitation of such an approach is that inter-cluster edges are discarded, severing long-range dependencies. This might be limiting on long-range tasks.

Contributions.

We propose CoRe-GNN (Coarsen and Restore), an architecture that performs in parallel an inter-cluster propagation on the coarsened graph and an intra-cluster propagation on the original node space, coupling the two across layers. The architecture is agnostic to the choice of the coarsening algorithm, which is treated as a tunable hyperparameter. This design addresses simultaneously the accuracy ceiling of graph coarsening and the long-range blindness of Cluster-GCN. First, we provide a unified matrix formulation of compressed-graph GNN training, showing that Cluster-GCN and graph coarsening correspond to complementary structured modifications of the propagation matrix S{S}, clarifying their limitations and motivating CoRe-GNN. Second, we introduce a natural batching scheme that scales CoRe-GNN to graphs with millions of nodes. Third, we prove that CoRe-GNN inherits guarantees over the preservation of smooth signal propagation, with the same structure as those of graph coarsening but with different multiplicative constants that we empirically evaluate. Fourth, we evaluate CoRe-GNN on homophilic, heterophilic, large-scale, and long-range node classification benchmarks, consistently outperforming Cluster-GCN and graph coarsening baselines. An illustrative diagram of the method can be found in Fig. 1.

Related work.

Of course, there are many other classes of methods to handle large graphs. Sampling-based methods address the ll-hop explosion by approximating the neighborhood of a node at each layer. GraphSAGE [13] samples a fixed number of neighbors per layer for each node in a batch. The number of sampled neighbors grows exponentially with the number of layers making deep architectures expensive, and a large body of work has been devoted to mitigating this cost [3, 39, 11]. An alternative is to sample entire subgraphs rather than individual neighbors [37, 36]. In general, coarsening-based and sampling-based methods differ structurally: while coarsening is performed once before training as a pre-processing, sampling is generally performed at every step of training, thus requiring to retain access to the original graph. Graph pooling methods [35, 1] are designed for graph-level classification and do not support node-level prediction. Most are differentiable and learned end-to-end, in contrast to the fixed pre-computed partitions used in coarsening-based approaches. Graph U-Net [10] extends pooling to node classification but its differentiable coarsening is memory-intensive and not designed for scalability. Graph condensation [15] creates a small synthetic graph by aligning GNN gradients between the compressed and original graphs. While effective at small reduction ratios, it does not preserve the original topology and evaluation on the full graph at inference remains memory-intensive. Graph summarization encompasses broader compression techniques: VQ-GNN [8] compresses node representations via vector quantization, while methods based on overlapping cluster structures [9, 21] allow nodes to belong to multiple communities simultaneously. Several works use multi-level aggregation across different graph resolutions [38, 23], but rely on complex aggregation schemes that are not batchable and do not target scalability to large graphs. In our work, the two levels of granularity serve a different purpose: resolving the accuracy ceiling of coarsening-only methods while preserving the scalability benefits of the cluster partition. Close to our work, FiT-GNN [28] and [32] treat coarsened nodes as auxiliary nodes appended to the original graph, keeping all computations in the original node space. This avoids the dimension change between original and coarsened spaces but does not benefit from the computational advantages of training and inferring within the coarsened space.

2 Compressed-Graph GNNs as Propagation Matrix Modifications

Several compressed-graph GNN methods can be written as modifications of the standard update (1), replacing S{S} by a structurally modified matrix to reduce memory and computation:

H(l)=σ⁡(Scompressed​H(l−1)​θ(l))H^{(l)}=\sigma\left(S_{\mathrm{compressed}}\,H^{(l-1)}\theta^{(l)}\right) (2)

We detail below two such methods, Coarsen-GNN [17, 16] and Cluster-GCN [4], which operate on complementary modifications of the same partition-based decomposition of S{S}. Note that both Coarsen-GNN and Cluster-GCN refer here to training and evaluating a GNN on, respectively, a coarsened or a clustered version of a graph, computed as a pre-processing with a dedicated algorithm (see Sec. 4), not to using a GNN to learn the coarsening or the clustering.

2.1 Coarsen-GNN

Graph coarsening [25, 16] reduces a graph GG with NN nodes to a coarsened graph GcG_{c} with n<Nn<N nodes. The proportion of reduction achieved is measured by the coarsening ratio r=1−nNr=1-\frac{n}{N}. The mapping from GG to GcG_{c} is obtained by grouping set of nodes in GG to form so-called supernodes in GcG_{c}. Following [16], we describe the coarsening through two matrices: a reduction matrix P∈ℝn×NP\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times N}, which allows going from the original NN-dimensional space to the coarsened nn-dimensional space, and a lifting matrix Q∈ℝN×nQ\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times n}, which allows going back. Perhaps surprisingly, it is more convenient to define the coarsening through the lifting matrix QQ, while PP will naturally follow [16]. First, QQ must be well-partitioned: it must have exactly one non-zero entry per row, ensuring each original node ii belongs to exactly one supernode ℓ\ell, when Qi​ℓ>0Q_{i\ell}>0. Second, the non-zero entries of QQ are chosen such that, given some symmetric Laplacian LL on GG, the coarsened Laplacian Lc=Q⊤​L​QL_{c}=Q^{\top}LQ is well-defined as a true Laplacian. Examples include the combinatorial Laplacian D−AD-A or the self-loop normalized Laplacian [16] L=(D+I)−1/2(D−A)(D+I)−1/2L=(D+I)^{-1/2}(D-A)(D+I)^{-1/2}, which is related to the propagation matrix SS in GCN [20]. We generally adopt the latter in this paper. There are several possible choices for PP [16], but the most natural is to set P=Q+P=Q^{+}, the Moore-Penrose pseudo-inverse of QQ. Since QQ is well-partitioned, Q+=(Q⊤​Q)−1​Q⊤Q^{+}=(Q^{\top}Q)^{-1}Q^{\top} has only NN non-zero elements, resulting in linear-complexity lifting and reduction operations. In this paper we will always consider that P=Q+P=Q^{+}.

Coarsen-GNN performs the entire propagation directly on the coarsened graph of size nn. Considering node representations Hc(l)∈ℝn×dH_{c}^{(l)}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times d} on the coarsened graph, with initial Hc(0)=P​H(0)H^{(0)}_{c}=PH^{(0)}, the propagation is naturally

Coarsen-GNN:Hc(l)=σ⁡(Sc​Hc(l−1)​θ(l))\text{Coarsen-GNN}:\quad H_{c}^{(l)}=\sigma\!\left(S_{c}\,H_{c}^{(l-1)}\theta^{(l)}\right) (3)

where Sc=P​S​Q∈ℝn×nS_{c}=PSQ\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n} is the propagation matrix introduced in [17], followed by a final lifting by QQ. Since QQ commutes with any pointwise activation σ\sigma (Lemma 1) and P​Q=InPQ=I_{n}, (3) can equivalently be rewritten as a propagation on the original graph with the matrix Π​S​Π\Pi S\Pi, where Π=Q​P∈ℝN×N\Pi=QP\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times N} is the coarsen-lift operator:

H(l)=σ⁡(Π​S​Π​H(l−1)​θ(l))=Q​σ​(Sc​P​H(l−1)​θ(l))H^{(l)}=\sigma\!\left(\Pi S\Pi\,H^{(l-1)}\theta^{(l)}\right)=Q\sigma\!\left({S_{c}}\,PH^{(l-1)}\theta^{(l)}\right) (4)

This shows that Coarsen-GNN fits the general framework (2) with Scompressed=Π​S​ΠS_{\mathrm{compressed}}=\Pi S\Pi. Of course, in practice, Coarsen-GNN propagates Hc(l)H_{c}^{(l)} and only maps the final predictions back to the original nodes, but this view is a stepping stone towards our more general architecture. Moreover, it outlines the main limitation of Coarsen-GNN: since Π\Pi is constant by block, all nodes within the same supernode receive the same prediction. As most coarsening algorithms merge neighboring nodes, this is particularly limiting on heterophilic graphs where adjacent nodes often carry different labels.

2.2 Cluster-GCN

Cluster-GCN [4] also operates on a partitioning of the graph, here more classically referred to as clusters (instead of “supernodes”). Rather than projecting the node representations into a smaller space, it restricts the propagation to intra-cluster connections only, that is, it removes all edges between clusters. Denoting SintraS^{\mathrm{intra}} the restriction of S{S} to intra-cluster connections, Cluster-GCN replaces S{S} by SintraS^{\mathrm{intra}} at every layer:

Cluster-GCN:H(l)=σ⁡(Sintra​H(l−1)​θ(l))\text{Cluster-GCN}:\quad H^{(l)}=\sigma\!\left(S^{\mathrm{intra}}\,H^{(l-1)}\theta^{(l)}\right) (5)

In addition to saving memory by discarding some connections, the main advantage of Cluster-GCN is that, since SintraS^{\mathrm{intra}} is block-diagonal with one block per cluster, batching is straightforward: at each training step, we can select a subset ℬ\mathcal{B} of clusters and loads only the corresponding blocks of SintraS^{\mathrm{intra}} and node representations. However, Cluster-GCN severs all inter-cluster and long-range dependencies, which severely limits its performance on long-range tasks [24].

Figure 2 illustrates the propagation matrices of the different methods.

Remark 1.

Note that the original Cluster-GCN paper [4] also considers merging several randomly drawn clusters per batch during training, but similar to Coarsen-GNN here we consider that the partitioning is fixed, done as a preprocessing step.

3 A new architecture CoRe-GNN

We have seen above that Coarsen-GNN assigns a single representation per supernode, limiting per-node discriminability, while Cluster-GCN discards all inter-cluster connections, severing long-range dependencies. In some sense, these are complementary limitations, which we simultaneously address with the proposed CoRe-GNN. It combines both strategies in parallel: it adds intra-cluster connections to Coarsen-GNN, or equivalently, extends Cluster-GCN with coarsened inter-cluster propagation. Denoting Sinter=S−SintraS^{\mathrm{inter}}={S}-S^{\mathrm{intra}} the inter-cluster part of S{S} and Scinter=P​Sinter​Q∈ℝn×nS^{\mathrm{inter}}_{c}=PS^{\mathrm{inter}}Q\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n} its coarsened counterpart, CoRe-GNN performs both propagations in parallel at each layer:

CoRe-GNN:H(l)=Q​σ​(Scinter​P​H(l−1)​θc(l))+σ⁡(Sintra​H(l−1)​θ(l))\text{CoRe-GNN}:\quad H^{(l)}=Q\,\sigma\!\left(S^{\mathrm{inter}}_{c}\,PH^{(l-1)}\theta_{c}^{(l)}\right)+\sigma\!\left(S^{\mathrm{intra}}\,H^{(l-1)}\theta^{(l)}\right) (6)

The name CoRe-GNN reflects this two-step structure, where the inter-cluster term coarsens the signal to capture long-range structure, while the intra-cluster term restores per-node discriminability lost by the coarsening. Unlike Coarsen-GNN which maps back to the original dimension only at the final layer, CoRe-GNN couples the two spaces at every layer via QQ and PP, maintaining two parallel states Hc(l)H_{c}^{(l)} and H(l)H^{(l)}, which directly motivates the batching scheme presented right after. An illustrative diagram is provided in Figure 1. The weight matrices θ(l)\theta^{(l)} and θc(l)\theta_{c}^{(l)} are independent: they respectively treat close-by intra-connections and long-range coarsened connections. Several design choices including weight sharing are studied in Appendix D.

Remark 2 (CoRe-GNN strictly generalizes Cluster-GCN and approximates Coarsen-GNN).

Setting θc(l)=0\theta_{c}^{(l)}=0 in CoRe-GNN recovers Cluster-GCN exactly. The converse direction is more subtle: setting θ(l)=0\theta^{(l)}=0 does not recover Coarsen-GNN, as Scinter=P​Sinter​QS^{\mathrm{inter}}_{c}=PS^{\mathrm{inter}}Q differs from Sc=P​S​Q{S_{c}}=PSQ by the term P​Sintra​QPS^{\mathrm{intra}}Q. This term is block-diagonal as shown in Lemma 2.

3.1 Natural Batching extension

CoRe-GNN is designed to scale to large graphs where classical GCN runs out of GPU memory. Although the proposed architecture is already lighter than full GCN by replacing S{S} by the sparser combination Sintra+Q​Scinter​PS^{\mathrm{intra}}+QS^{\mathrm{inter}}_{c}P, this alone is not sufficient to handle graphs with millions of nodes. However, akin to Cluster-GCN, CoRe-GNN is amenable to a natural batching strategy, by only selecting some clusters for intra-propagation. The batching scheme maintains two parallel states: Hc(l)H_{c}^{(l)} for all super-nodes in the coarsened space, and Hℬ(l)H_{\mathcal{B}}^{(l)} for the batched nodes only, in the original space. At each step, the inter-cluster term runs over all nn super-nodes cheaply since n≪Nn\ll N, while only the clusters in the current batch ℬ\mathcal{B} perform the full intra-cluster propagation. For non-batch super-nodes, the intra-cluster term is approximated by a self-loop proxy in the coarsened space, which is equivalent to lifting the super-node to the original space, applying a self-loop node by node, and reducing back.

Algorithm 1 summarizes the batched forward pass. A custom sampler groups clusters until a target node count is reached, ensuring constant-size batches despite variable cluster sizes. The intra-cluster blocks are pre-split at loading time and remain fixed during training, so no graph partitioning or subgraph sampling is performed during training.

Exact inference.

Without batches, standard full-graph inference of CoRe-GNN may be out of memory on very large graphs such as Reddit and OGBN-Products [14], even without retaining gradients. However, we can derive a non-trivial exact inference procedure that avoids this bottleneck without any approximation, without resorting to the self-loop proxy used during training. For each layer, the inter-cluster term is computed once over all nn super-nodes on GPU via ScinterS^{\mathrm{inter}}_{c}, while the intra-cluster term is computed cluster by cluster, loading each block Sintra​[ℬ]S^{\mathrm{intra}}[\mathcal{B}] from CPU to GPU on demand and discarding it immediately after. This strategy is not applicable during training, since backpropagation requires retaining the full computational graph across all layers, which causes out-of-memory crashes on large graphs. Detailed pseudo-codes for exact inference (Appendix E.1), Coarsen-GNN training, CoRe-GNN full batch and batched training are provided in Appendix E.

3.2 Complexity

CoRe-GNN replaces the full propagation matrix S{S} by the sparser combination Sintra+Q​Scinter​PS^{\mathrm{intra}}+QS^{\mathrm{inter}}_{c}P. Classical GCN requires 𝒪⁡(K​E​d+K​N​d2)\mathcal{O}(KEd+KNd^{2}) operations per epoch, where KK is the number of layers, E=nnz⁡(S)E=\mathrm{nnz}({S}) the number of edges, and dd the hidden dimension. CoRe-GNN substitutes EE by Eintra+EcE_{\mathrm{intra}}+E_{c}, where Eintra=nnz⁡(Sintra)≤EE_{\mathrm{intra}}=\mathrm{nnz}(S^{\mathrm{intra}})\leq E and Ec=nnz⁡(Scinter)≪EE_{c}=\mathrm{nnz}(S^{\mathrm{inter}}_{c})\ll E since Scinter∈ℝn×nS^{\mathrm{inter}}_{c}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n} with n≪Nn\ll N. The lifting and reduction operations via PP and QQ, which have only NN non-zero elements each, add a negligible 𝒪⁡(N)\mathcal{O}(N) cost. Whether CoRe-GNN is cheaper than classical GCN depends on the graph structure and the coarsening ratio, as analyzed in Appendix C.2. The batched variant provides a more systematic advantage: memory is reduced to 𝒪⁡(K⁡(n+b)​d)\mathcal{O}(K(n+b)d), independent of NN, enabling training on graphs that would otherwise exceed GPU memory. A detailed complexity table of all methods is also provided in Appendix C.

3.3 Propagation guarantees for CoRe-GNN

In this section, we derive some theoretical guarantees that bound the error between message-passing on the original graph and message-passing in CoRe-GNN. For this, we adapt the results in [17] for Coarsen-GNN. Note that, to our knowledge, there is no theoretical analysis for Cluster-GCN that we could adapt for CoRe-GNN, and we leave such a complementary approach for future work.

In this section LL denotes a symmetric Laplacian of the original graph, the propagation matrix is S=IN−LS=I_{N}-L, and QQ is such that the coarsened Laplacian Lc=Q⊤​L​QL_{c}=Q^{\top}LQ is well-defined. Recall that P=Q+P=Q^{+} and Π=Q​P\Pi=QP. For a symmetric positive semi-definite matrix LL, we define the Mahalanobis semi-norm ‖x‖L=x⊤​L​x\|x\|_{L}=\sqrt{x^{\top}Lx} and the associated pseudo-operator norm ∥M∥L=∥L1/2ML−1/2∥o​p\|M\|_{L}=\|L^{1/2}ML^{-1/2}\|_{op}.

Reminder on Coarsening guarantee.

To measure the quality of a coarsening, Loukas [25] introduced the Restricted Spectral Approximation (RSA) constant, which measures the loss of information from a signal xx to its coarsened and re-lifted counterpart x~=Π​x\tilde{x}=\Pi x. Since Π\Pi is at most of rank n<Nn<N, only a subspace ℛ\mathcal{R} of ℝN\mathbb{R}^{N} can be preserved exactly.

Definition 1 (Restricted Spectral Approximation constant).

Given a subspace ℛ⊂ℝN\mathcal{R}\subset\mathbb{R}^{N}, a Laplacian LL, a lifting matrix QQ and a reduction matrix PP, the RSA constant is:

ϵL,Q,P,ℛ=supx∈ℛ,‖x‖L=1∥x−Q​P​x∥L\epsilon_{L,Q,P,\mathcal{R}}=\sup_{x\in\mathcal{R},\,\|x\|_{L}=1}\lVert x-QPx\rVert_{L} (7)

Classically, ℛ\mathcal{R} is spanned by the eigenvectors associated with the smallest eigenvalues of LL, corresponding to the smoothest signals on the graph. Then, the authors in [17] show that, with our choice of propagation matrix Sc=P​S​Q{S_{c}}=PSQ, one step of message-passing in Coarsen-GNN (3) is provably close to message-passing on the original graph, in terms of the RSA constant ϵL,Q,P,ℛ\epsilon_{L,Q,P,\mathcal{R}}.

Theorem 1 (Propagation on coarsened graph [17]).

Under the assumption that Π\Pi and SS are both ker⁡(L)\ker(L)-preserving and SS is ℛ\mathcal{R}-preserving, for all x∈ℛx\in\mathcal{R}:

∥S​x−Q​Sc​P​x∥L≤ϵL,Q,P,ℛ​∥x∥L​(CS+CΠ)\lVert Sx-Q{S_{c}}Px\rVert_{L}\leq\epsilon_{L,Q,P,\mathcal{R}}\lVert x\rVert_{L}\left(C_{S}+C_{\Pi}\right) (8)

where CS:=∥S∥LC_{S}:=\lVert S\rVert_{L}, CΠ:=∥Π​S∥LC_{\Pi}:=\lVert\Pi S\rVert_{L}, and MM is said EE-preserving if M​x∈EMx\in E for all x∈Ex\in E.

The various assumptions of Theorem 1 are discussed in the original paper [17]. The RSA constant controls how well the coarsened graph preserves smooth signals, which directly justifies using coarsening algorithms that minimize the RSA [25] rather than other spectral criteria.

Guarantees for CoRe-GNN.

Theorem 1 extends naturally to CoRe-GNN, under the same assumptions but with different constants. The full derivation is in Appendix A.1.

Theorem 2 (Propagation guarantee for CoRe-GNN).

Under the assumption that Π\Pi and SinterS^{\mathrm{inter}} are both ker⁡(L)\ker(L)-preserving and SinterS^{\mathrm{inter}} is ℛ\mathcal{R}-preserving, for all x∈ℛx\in\mathcal{R}:

∥S​x−(Sintra​x+Q​Scinter​P​x)∥L≤ϵL,Q,P,ℛ​∥x∥L​(CS′+CΠ′)\lVert Sx-\left(S^{\mathrm{intra}}x+QS^{\mathrm{inter}}_{c}Px\right)\rVert_{L}\leq\epsilon_{L,Q,P,\mathcal{R}}\lVert x\rVert_{L}\left(C_{S}^{\prime}+C_{\Pi}^{\prime}\right) (9)

where CS′:=∥Sinter∥LC_{S}^{\prime}:=\lVert S^{\mathrm{inter}}\rVert_{L}, CΠ′:=∥Π​Sinter∥LC_{\Pi}^{\prime}:=\lVert\Pi S^{\mathrm{inter}}\rVert_{L}.

The constants CS′C_{S}^{\prime} and CΠ′C_{\Pi}^{\prime} now depend on SinterS^{\mathrm{inter}} rather than SS. Comparing the two results, CoRe-GNN has better preservation guarantees than Coarsen-GNN when CS′+CΠ′<CS+CΠC_{S}^{\prime}+C_{\Pi}^{\prime}<C_{S}+C_{\Pi}. While there is no guarantee that this is always the case, as these constants involves operator norms, note that if we consider Frobenius norms instead we would easily have ∥Sinter∥Fro≤∥S∥Fro\lVert S^{\mathrm{inter}}\rVert_{\mathrm{Fro}}\leq\lVert S\rVert_{\mathrm{Fro}}, hinting that the constants are indeed improved for CoRe-GNN. A notable difference is that CS′=∥Sinter∥LC_{S}^{\prime}=\lVert S^{\mathrm{inter}}\rVert_{L} depends on the coarsening, while CS=∥S∥LC_{S}=\lVert S\rVert_{L} is fixed by the graph. As the coarsening ratio increases, SinterS^{\mathrm{inter}} becomes sparser and CS′C_{S}^{\prime} is expected to decrease.

Figure 3 shows the constants CSC_{S}, CΠC_{\Pi}, CS′C^{\prime}_{S}, CΠ′C^{\prime}_{\Pi}, the full theoretical upper bound, as well as the empirical propagation error averaged over 100 signals sampled from the low-frequency eigenvectors of LL, as a function of the coarsening ratio rr, on an SBM synthetic graph. We observe that the theoretical bound and the propagation error are consistently lower for CoRe-GNN across all coarsening ratios. On real graphs (see Appendix B), the picture is more nuanced: the constants for CoRe-GNN are not always smaller, but the empirical propagation error generally remains lower, showing that the upper bounds of Theorem 1 and 2 tend to be rather loose on real data.

4 Experimental results

Setup.

CoRe-GNN and its batched variant are designed for node classification on medium to large-scale graphs. All experiments are run on a single NVIDIA A40 GPU for reproducibility, and out-of-memory (OOM) results correspond to the memory limit of this hardware. All results are averaged over 10 runs.

(i) Coarsening algorithms: we consider three possible algorithms to partition the graph into supernodes/clusters. METIS [18] minimizes the normalized cut between clusters and produces balanced partitions with a very efficient implementation. Graclus [6] minimizes the ratio cut via a multilevel approach and is applied iteratively to approach the target coarsening ratio. Loukas [25] is designed to minimize the RSA for the self-loop normalized Laplacian, as implemented in [17, 16]. We report results for the best-performing algorithm per dataset and per model. Pseudo-codes and implementation details are provided in Appendix G. The coarsening ratio rr is also a tunable hyperparameter, constrained by available GPU memory. In contrast to Coarsen-GNN, increasing rr does not systematically reduce the computational cost of CoRe-GNN. While larger values of rr reduce the size of the coarsened graph, they also lead to larger clusters, increasing the number of intra-cluster connections and potentially causing memory issues. This reflects a trade-off in rr, as further detailed in Appendix C.2. For all reported results, we select the best coarsening ratio rr per model and dataset.

(ii) Models. We evaluate CoRe-GNN and its batched variant CoRe-GNN(b). As CoRe-GNN approximates the full GCN propagation, we compare against full GCN [20] when memory allows. We also compare against our implementation of Cluster-GCN, which performs only intra-cluster propagation and Coarsen-GNN [17, 16], which trains and infers entirely on the coarsened graph. Our goal is to evaluate the effect of the propagation structure rather than to maximize benchmark scores, and we therefore do not include architecture-specific tricks such as residual connections.

(iii) Hyperparameters. All models are trained with the Adam optimizer for up to 800 epochs with a ReduceLROnPlateau scheduler and a dropout of 0.50.5. Each model is evaluated over a hyperparameter grid covering hidden dimension, number of layers, learning rate, weight decay, and coarsening ratio where applicable. The grid varies per model and dataset group. Full hyperparameter grids and per-dataset selected values are provided in Appendix H.

Influence of coarsening ratio.

While in the main tables we select the best coarsening ratio for each model, Figure 4 reports accuracy as a function of rr on Cora with fixed hyperparameters. At low ratios, clusters are small as there are many super-nodes, and Coarsen-GNN preserves per-node discriminability well, peaking at r=0.3r=0.3 (max 81.53%81.53\%). At higher coarsening ratios, accuracy drops as more nodes share the same prediction, although these regimes are precisely those where coarsening is computationally most beneficial. In contrast, Cluster-GCN performs poorly at low ratios, where clusters are too small for effective intra-cluster propagation, and improves as rr increases. However, at very high ratios, each cluster approaches the full graph, which removes the benefit of batching and can lead to memory issues. Peak performance is reached at r=0.999r=0.999 (81.17%81.17\%). CoRe-GNN’s strong performance across all ratios, with a peak accuracy of 81.62%81.62\% at r=0.4r=0.4, suggests that combining both propagation mechanisms mitigates this trade-off.

Homophilic datasets.

We evaluate on the three Planetoid citation networks [34]: Cora, Citeseer and Pubmed. We restrict to the main connected component of Cora and Citeseer, which may explain small differences with other benchmarks. On Cora and Citeseer, Coarsen-GNN achieves the best mean accuracy, while CoRe-GNN is a close second. Both outperform full GCN, as coarsening preserves low-frequency graph structure that aligns well with homophilic label distributions. On Pubmed, CoRe-GNN ranks first. These datasets are not particularly challenging for coarsening-based methods, as clusters tend to be label-homogeneous.

Heterophilic datasets.

We consider Chameleon, Squirrel [29] and Amazon Ratings [27]. On these datasets, Coarsen-GNN is limited by its constant-by-block predictions: as most coarsening algorithms merge neighboring nodes, nodes within the same supernode often carry different labels, directly capping accuracy. CoRe-GNN significantly outperforms Coarsen-GNN on all three datasets. As shown in recent benchmarks [26], heterophilic graphs require long-range information to be classified accurately, which explains why CoRe-GNN also outperforms Cluster-GCN. On Squirrel, full GCN outperforms CoRe-GNN, while CoRe-GNN(b) achieves the best results, suggesting that the batching scheme provides additional regularization on this dataset.

Large-scale graphs.

We report results on ogbn-arxiv [14], Reddit [13] and ogbn-products [14]. On ogbn-arxiv, Coarsen-GNN performs poorly as the graph has weak community structure, while CoRe-GNN and Cluster-GCN are both competitive but do not surpass full GCN. On Reddit and ogbn-products, full GCN and CoRe-GNN without batching are out of memory. CoRe-GNN(b) significantly outperforms both Cluster-GCN and Coarsen-GNN on these datasets, suggesting that the inter-cluster and intra-cluster propagations capture complementary information.

Long-range tasks.

We evaluate on the Paris and London road networks [24], two recently introduced large graphs specifically designed to measure long-range interactions in graph machine learning. A description of all datasets is provided in Appendix F. These graphs require aggregating information over many hops to correctly classify nodes, making them particularly challenging for local message passing methods. Among the baselines, Coarsen-GNN outperforms both Cluster-GCN and full GCN as its inter-cluster propagation already captures some long-range structure. CoRe-GNN and CoRe-GNN(b) achieve the best accuracy among the architectures considered here, indicating that combining inter- and intra-cluster propagations provides the most effective long-range aggregation in this setting.

5 Conclusion

CoRe-GNN combines inter-cluster and intra-cluster propagations in parallel at each layer, overcoming the limitations of both graph coarsening and Cluster-GCN. The architecture is agnostic to the choice of coarsening algorithm, admits a natural batching scheme that scales to graphs with millions of nodes, and inherits provable propagation guarantees from graph coarsening. On node classification benchmarks spanning homophilic, heterophilic, large-scale, and long-range graphs, CoRe-GNN consistently outperforms both Coarsen-GNN and Cluster-GCN baselines, and achieves substantial gains over full GCN on long-range tasks on the cities datasets.

Limitations and outlook.

The unified matrix formulation underlying CoRe-GNN applies to GNNs whose forward pass can be expressed through a fixed propagation matrix S{S}, excluding architectures with residual connections or learned propagation matrices such as Graph Attention Networks [31]. Adapting CoRe-GNN to these settings is a natural direction for future work, alongside using separate optimizers for the two branches and designing residual connections compatible with the two-branch structure. On the theoretical side, a multi-level extension where the coarsened graph is itself coarsened recursively would naturally generalize the architecture.

Beyond these extensions, CoRe-GNN (batched) also suggests a natural connection to asynchronous federated learning. The coarsened graph plays the role of a central aggregator that receives local updates from the clusters selected in the current batch. For clusters that have not yet reported back, the central aggregator sends a self-loop proxy in place of their local update. This asynchronous communication pattern suggests that CoRe-GNN could serve as a framework for federated GNN training on large graphs, where not all agents are available at each round.

Appendix B Analysis of Propagation Bound Constants

This section provides a deeper analysis of the constants CSC_{S}, CΠC_{\Pi}, CS′C_{S}^{\prime} and CΠ′C_{\Pi}^{\prime} appearing in Theorems 1 and 2. For each graph, we plot the four quantities: CSC_{S} and CΠC_{\Pi} terms, full theoretical upper bound, and mean propagation error averaged over 100 smooth signals sampled from the low-frequency subspace of LL, all as a function of the coarsening ratio rr, comparing Coarsen-GNN (blue) and CoRe-GNN (red). We first analyze four SBM graphs with varying community structure (Section B.1), then four real datasets (Section B.2), before discussing the results(Section B.3).

B.1 Empirical analysis on SBM graphs

We analyze the bounds on four synthetic Stochastic Block Model (SBM) graphs, each with 5 communities of 100 nodes. In an SBM, edges are drawn independently with probability pinp_{\rm in} within communities and poutp_{\rm out} across communities. We vary pinp_{\rm in} and poutp_{\rm out} to span a range of spectral connectivities. SBM-1 and SBM-2 are sparse graphs with low pinp_{\rm in}, while SBM-3 and SBM-4 are denser with higher inter-community connectivity. All graphs are coarsened with the Loukas algorithm. For each graph we show its structure and the four bound quantities as a function of the coarsening ratio rr. SBM-2 corresponds to the graph shown in the main paper (Figure 3).

B.2 Empirical analysis on real graphs

We repeat the same analysis on four real datasets: Cora, Citeseer, Chameleon and Squirrel.

B.3 Discussion

Across all graphs and coarsening ratios, the mean propagation error averaged over smooth signals is consistently lower for CoRe-GNN than for Coarsen-GNN, even when the theoretical bound constants are not strictly smaller. This gap between the bound and the true error is expected: the bound is a worst-case quantity while the mean error reflects typical behavior on low-frequency signals, which are precisely the signals preserved by spectral coarsening. Heterophily does not affect this analysis, as we sample signals from the low-frequency subspace of LL regardless of the graph’s label structure.

Appendix C Detailed Complexity Analysis

This section provides a detailed complexity analysis of all methods considered in this paper. Table 3 summarizes time and memory complexity, and Section C.2 analyzes the regimes in which CoRe-GNN is theoretically cheaper than classical GCN.

C.1 Complexity table

Table 3 summarizes the time and memory complexity of each method. We use KK for the number of layers, dd for the hidden dimension, NN for the number of nodes, E=nnz⁡(S)E=\mathrm{nnz}({S}) for the number of edges, n=(1−r)​Nn=(1-r)N for the number of super-nodes at coarsening ratio rr, Ec=nnz⁡(Scinter)E_{c}=\mathrm{nnz}(S^{\mathrm{inter}}_{c}) for the number of edges in the coarsened graph, Eintra=nnz⁡(Sintra)E_{\mathrm{intra}}=\mathrm{nnz}(S^{\mathrm{intra}}) for the number of intra-cluster edges, bb for the batch size in nodes and nbatchn_{\mathrm{batch}} for the number of batches per epoch.

Classical GCN.

At each of the KK layers, the sparse matrix-vector product S​H(l−1){S}H^{(l-1)} costs 𝒪⁡(E​d)\mathcal{O}(Ed) and the linear transformation costs 𝒪⁡(N​d2)\mathcal{O}(Nd^{2}). Storing all intermediate representations for backpropagation requires 𝒪⁡(K​N​d)\mathcal{O}(KNd) memory.

Coarsen-GNN.

Training operates entirely in the coarsened space of nn nodes and EcE_{c} edges, with memory 𝒪⁡(K​n​d)\mathcal{O}(Knd). The lifting operation Q​Hc(K)QH_{c}^{(K)} at the final layer costs 𝒪⁡(N​d)\mathcal{O}(Nd) due to the sparsity of QQ, adding an 𝒪⁡(N​d)\mathcal{O}(Nd) memory term for storing the lifted predictions.

Cluster-GCN.

Only intra-cluster edges are used, replacing EE by Eintra≤EE_{\mathrm{intra}}\leq E in the temporal complexity. The memory complexity is 𝒪⁡(K​b​d)\mathcal{O}(Kbd) per batch since only bb node representations are stored at any time.

CoRe-GNN.

Each layer performs both the inter-cluster propagation in the coarsened space at cost 𝒪⁡(Ec​d+n​d2)\mathcal{O}(E_{c}d+nd^{2}) and the intra-cluster propagation at cost 𝒪⁡(Eintra​d+N​d2)\mathcal{O}(E_{\mathrm{intra}}d+Nd^{2}), plus two lifting and reduction operations at cost 𝒪⁡(N​d)\mathcal{O}(Nd) each due to the sparsity of PP and QQ. Memory stores two sets of representations: 𝒪⁡(K​N​d)\mathcal{O}(KNd) for the original space and 𝒪⁡(K​n​d)\mathcal{O}(Knd) for the coarsened space.

CoRe-GNN batched.

The intra-cluster term is computed over the batch of bb nodes only, summing to 𝒪⁡(K⁡(Eintra​d+N​d2))\mathcal{O}(K(E_{\mathrm{intra}}d+Nd^{2})) over all batches. The inter-cluster term is recomputed for each of the nbatchn_{\mathrm{batch}} batches per epoch, contributing 𝒪⁡(K​nbatch​(Ec​d+n​d2))\mathcal{O}(Kn_{\mathrm{batch}}(E_{c}d+nd^{2})), where the d2d^{2} term accounts for the linear transformation in the coarsened space recomputed at each batch, giving a total time complexity of 𝒪⁡(K⁡(nbatch​Ec​d+Eintra​d+(nbatch+N)​d2))\mathcal{O}(K(n_{\mathrm{batch}}E_{c}d+E_{\mathrm{intra}}d+(n_{\mathrm{batch}}+N)d^{2})). The key advantage over all compared architectures is that memory complexity is 𝒪⁡(K⁡(n+b)​d)\mathcal{O}(K(n+b)d), independent of NN, making large-scale training tractable even when the full graph does not fit on GPU.

C.2 Efficiency regimes for CoRe-GNN

CoRe-GNN has a lower theoretical time complexity than classical GCN when:

Ec+Eintra+2​N+n​d≤EE_{c}+E_{\mathrm{intra}}+2N+nd\leq E (18)

Neither EcE_{c} nor EintraE_{\mathrm{intra}} admits a closed-form expression as a function of NN and rr alone, as both depend on the graph structure and the coarsening algorithm. We analyze one tractable case below and then verify the condition empirically on a medium scale sparse graph ogbn-arxiv.

Dense graphs with balanced partitions.

To build intuition in a tractable theoretical setting, we analyze the efficiency condition under two simplifying assumptions: the original graph is dense with E=N2E=N^{2}, and the coarsening produces balanced clusters of equal size N/n=1/(1−r)N/n=1/(1-r). Under these assumptions, each cluster forms a clique of size N/nN/n, giving Eintra=n⋅(N/n)2=N2/n=N/(1−r)E_{\mathrm{intra}}=n\cdot(N/n)^{2}=N^{2}/n=N/(1-r), and in the worst case the coarsened graph is also complete with Ec=n2=(1−r)2​N2E_{c}=n^{2}=(1-r)^{2}N^{2}. Condition (18) then becomes:

(1−r)2​N2+N1−r+2​N+(1−r)​N​d≤N2(1-r)^{2}N^{2}+\frac{N}{1-r}+2N+(1-r)Nd\leq N^{2}

For large NN with d≪Nd\ll N, the dominant terms are (1−r)2​N2(1-r)^{2}N^{2} on the left and N2N^{2} on the right, and the condition reduces to (1−r)2≤1(1-r)^{2}\leq 1, which holds for all r∈[0,1]r\in[0,1]. Dense graphs with balanced partitions therefore always satisfy the efficiency condition, regardless of the coarsening ratio, even in the worst case for EcE_{c}.

Empirical efficiency condition.

While the dense case is always favorable, graphs in practice are sparse. Figure 13 plots the left-hand side of condition (18) normalized by EE, using the actual values of EcE_{c} and EintraE_{\mathrm{intra}} computed from METIS coarsening on ogbn-arxiv (N=169,343N=169{,}343, E=1,166,243E=1{,}166{,}243), for d∈{64,128,256}d\in\{64,128,256\}. The condition is satisfied for sufficiently large rr, but at very high coarsening ratios EintraE_{\mathrm{intra}} grows back as clusters absorb more edges internally and the left-hand side increases again toward the threshold. On this medium-scale sparse graph the gains are moderate, and more pronounced improvements are expected on larger or denser graphs. We also recall that beyond time complexity, CoRe-GNN admits a natural batching scheme that addresses memory scalability independently of this condition.

Appendix D Ablation Study of CoRe-GNN

We study four design choices of CoRe-GNN: the normalization of the lifting matrix QQ (Table 4), the choice of inter-cluster propagation matrix (Table 5), weight sharing between the two branches (Table 6), and layer normalization (Table 7). All ablations are run with the same hyperparameters as the best results presented in the main manuscript, varying only the factor under study.

Normalization of the lifting matrix QQ.

The lifting matrix QQ can be defined in two ways. The combinatorial version 𝒬\mathcal{Q} has binary entries, with exactly one non-zero entry of value 11 per row. The normalized version uses Q=(D+I)−1/2𝒬(Dc+Ic)1/2Q=(D+I)^{-1/2}\mathcal{Q}(D_{c}+I_{c})^{1/2}, where DD and AA are the degree matrix and adjacency matrix of GG, and DcD_{c}, AcA_{c} their counterparts on GcG_{c}. This normalization is associated with the self-loop normalized Laplacian L=(D+I)−1/2(D−A)(D+I)−1/2L=(D+I)^{-1/2}(D-A)(D+I)^{-1/2}, which satisfies L=IN−SL=I_{N}-S. In both cases, P=Q+P=Q^{+} is the Moore-Penrose pseudoinverse of the chosen QQ, and both verify Lc=Q⊤​L​QL_{c}=Q^{\top}LQ and ℒc=Dc−Ac=𝒬⊤​ℒ​𝒬=𝒬⊤​(D−A)​𝒬\mathcal{L}_{c}=D_{c}-A_{c}=\mathcal{Q}^{\top}\mathcal{L}\mathcal{Q}=\mathcal{Q}^{\top}(D-A)\mathcal{Q}. Table 4 shows that the normalized variant performs better on most datasets, with a mean accuracy gain of +1.51%+1.51\%, and is used as default throughout the paper.

Choice of inter-cluster propagation matrix.

CoRe-GNN uses Scinter=P​Sinter​QS^{\mathrm{inter}}_{c}=PS^{\mathrm{inter}}Q as the inter-cluster propagation matrix, where Sinter=S−SintraS^{\mathrm{inter}}={S}-S^{\mathrm{intra}} contains only inter-cluster edges. An alternative is to use the full coarsened propagation matrix Sc=P​S​QS_{c}=PSQ, which additionally includes the intra-cluster term P​Sintra​QPS^{\mathrm{intra}}Q. Table 5 shows that ScinterS^{\mathrm{inter}}_{c} performs better on most datasets, with a mean accuracy gain of +2.62%+2.62\%. This is consistent with avoiding double-counting the intra-cluster contribution, which is already handled by the SintraS^{\mathrm{intra}} branch.

Weight sharing.

By default, CoRe-GNN uses independent weight matrices θ(l)\theta^{(l)} and θc(l)\theta_{c}^{(l)} for the intra-cluster and inter-cluster branches respectively. A simpler variant ties the two weights, setting θ(l)=θc(l)\theta^{(l)}=\theta_{c}^{(l)}. Table 6 shows that independent weights perform better on most datasets, with a mean accuracy gain of +2.30%+2.30\%. This suggests that the two branches benefit from learning distinct transformations, as the intra-cluster and inter-cluster propagations operate on different graph structures and at different scales.

Layer normalization.

Layer normalization normalizes representations across the feature dimension, independently of the number of nodes. This makes it compatible with our architecture where cluster sizes vary across batches, unlike batch normalization which depends on the number of nodes and would produce inconsistent statistics across batches of different sizes. Table 7 shows that the best choice is dataset-dependent: layer normalization is beneficial on Amazon Ratings and Paris, while the absence of normalization performs better on the remaining datasets. We therefore select the normalization setting per dataset during hyperparameter tuning.

Appendix E Pseudo code of Proposed methods

Algorithm 2 describes the training forward pass of Coarsen-GNN, which operates entirely in the coarsened space and maps the final predictions back to the original nodes.

Algorithm 3 describes the full batch training forward pass of CoRe-GNN, maintaining two parallel states Hc(l)H_{c}^{(l)} and H(l)H^{(l)} at each layer.

Algorithm 4 describes the batched training forward pass, where only the clusters selected in the current batch perform full intra-cluster propagation while the remaining super-nodes receive a self-loop proxy.

E.1 Pseudo-code of exact inference

Unlike training, exact inference introduces no approximation: every cluster is processed exactly, layer by layer. At each layer, Sintra​[ℬ]S^{\mathrm{intra}}[\mathcal{B}] is loaded batch by batch from CPU to GPU on demand, while H(l)H^{(l)} is written back to CPU after each layer to free GPU memory. This strategy is not applicable during training since backpropagation requires retaining the full computational graph across all layers, which is precisely why the self-loop proxy of Algorithm 1 is needed at training time.

Appendix F Datasets

We restrict Cora and Citeseer to their principal connected component (PCC) as coarsening algorithms tend to process small connected components first, leading to poor results at low coarsening ratios. This makes direct comparison with other benchmarks more difficult as the training and evaluation sets differ. The characteristics of these datasets and their PCC are reported in Table 8. Details for all datasets are in Table 9.

Homophilic datasets.

Cora, Citeseer and Pubmed [34] are citation networks where nodes are papers and edges are citations. Labels correspond to research topics and are strongly homophilic.

Heterophilic datasets.

Chameleon and Squirrel [29] are Wikipedia page networks. Amazon Ratings [27] is a co-purchase network where nodes are products. These datasets exhibit low homophily, making them challenging for local message passing methods.

Long-range datasets.

Paris and London [24] are road networks specifically designed to measure long-range interactions in graph machine learning.

Large-scale datasets.

ogbn-arxiv, Reddit [13] and ogbn-products [14] are large graphs with hundreds of thousands to millions of nodes, used to evaluate scalability.

Appendix G Coarsening Algorithms

We briefly describe the three coarsening algorithms used in this work. Among them, only METIS enforces balanced partitions by construction, while Graclus and Loukas do not impose cluster size constraints. Due to its higher computational cost, Loukas does not scale to very large graphs and was therefore not evaluated on ogbn-products.

METIS.

[18] partitions the graph into nn balanced clusters minimizing the normalized cut. Since METIS takes a target number of nodes as input rather than a ratio, we compute n=⌊(1−r)​N⌋n=\lfloor(1-r)N\rfloor from the desired coarsening ratio rr.

Graclus.

[6] applies a multilevel clustering based on the ratio cut. Since Graclus does not directly accept a target coarsening ratio, we apply it iteratively until n≤(1−r)​Nn\leq(1-r)N. The achieved ratio is therefore approximate, which makes this algorithm better suited to large graphs where small deviations in the number of super-nodes are acceptable.

G.1 Adaptation of Loukas Algorithm

The Loukas algorithm [25] constructs a coarsened graph by minimizing the RSA constant, ensuring that smooth signals on the original graph are well preserved after coarsening. Algorithm 6 presents our adaptation of the Loukas coarsening algorithm. The algorithm iteratively selects contraction sets, merges the corresponding nodes, and updates the graph structure. Our main modification replaces the combinatorial Laplacian by any Δ\Delta-Laplacian L=Δ​ℒ​ΔL=\Delta\mathcal{L}\Delta [16], and removes the diagonal of AcA_{c} at each iteration, which empirically yields lower RSA values.

Candidate contraction sets.

Contraction sets can be defined either as pairs of adjacent nodes (edge-based) or as full node neighborhoods. As neighborhoods tend to be large in our graphs, the neighborhood variant proves impractical at low coarsening ratios. We therefore use edge-based contraction sets and control the greedy behavior via nen_{e}.

Coarsening Hyperparameters of this paper

By default in this paper, LL is the self loop normalized laplacian L=(D+I)−1/2(D−A)(D+I)−1/2L=(D+I)^{-1/2}(D-A)(D+I)^{-1/2} such that S=IN−LS=I_{N}-L. The preserved space is the first KK eigenvectors of LL with K=100K=100. nen_{e} the number of edges contracted at each step is defined as 10%10\% of the original graph.

Appendix H Hyperparameters

H.1 Presentation of hyperparameters

All experiments use the Adam optimizer with a ReduceLROnPlateau scheduler, trained for up to 800 epochs with dropout fixed at 0.50.5 on a single NVIDIA A40 GPU. The hyperparameter grid covers the coarsening algorithm (METIS, Graclus, Loukas), coarsening ratio rr, hidden dimension, network depth KK, learning rate, weight decay, and layer normalization. Due to computational constraints, the full grid search was run over 3 seeds, while the final results reported in the main paper are averaged over 10 seeds.
